items.title: [Bug]: Telegram gateway platform force-enabled by TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN env, ignores config.yaml platforms.telegram.enabled: false

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Summary

Setting `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` in the environment unconditionally enables the Telegram gateway platform in `gateway/config.py`, **even when the user has explicitly set `platforms.telegram.enabled: false` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`**. There is no way to keep other Hermes features (skill bindings, prompt fragments, etc.) referencing a Telegram token while disabling the Telegram *gateway platform* itself (the polling listener).

This is the same root cause as #25065 (Home Assistant) and #47804 (Feishu) — the env-only activation wins. The systemic fix already exists for Slack (commit `156176a44`, refs #41112): a generalized `_enable_from_env` helper that respects the `_enabled_explicit` marker set by `config.yaml`. **Telegram just hasn't been migrated to that helper yet.**

## Affected code

Container image `hermes-saas:cortex` (built `2026-06-18T20:54:16Z`), `gateway/config.py` lines 1231-1236:

```python
# Telegram
telegram_token = os.getenv("TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN")
if telegram_token:
    if Platform.TELEGRAM not in config.platforms:
        config.platforms[Platform.TELEGRAM] = PlatformConfig()
    config.platforms[Platform.TELEGRAM].enabled = True   # <-- overrides config.yaml
    config.platforms[Platform.TELEGRAM].token = telegram_token
```

There is no check for `_enabled_explicit` and no consultation of `config.platforms[Platform.TELEGRAM].enabled`. The env var wins unconditionally.

## Suggested fix

Apply the same pattern Slack already uses (commit `156176a44`). In the local Hermes Agent checkout (`/home/cerebro/.hermes/hermes-agent/gateway/config.py`), `_apply_env_overrides` was refactored to use a helper:

```python
def _enable_from_env(platform: Platform) -> PlatformConfig:
    if platform not in config.platforms:
        config.platforms[platform] = PlatformConfig(enabled=True)
        return config.platforms[platform]
    platform_config = config.platforms[platform]
    enabled_was_explicit = bool(platform_config.extra.get("_enabled_explicit", False))
    if not platform_config.enabled and not enabled_was_explicit:
        platform_config.enabled = True
    return platform_config
```

Then Telegram becomes:

```python
telegram_token = os.getenv("TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN")
if telegram_token:
    telegram_config = _enable_from_env(Platform.TELEGRAM)
    telegram_config.token = telegram_token
```

## Why this matters: cascading consequences

When two Hermes installations (or one Hermes + one container) accidentally share the same `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`, both try to call `getUpdates` against the same bot. Telegram's long-poll API allows only ONE bot instance per token — second instance gets a `409 Conflict` immediately.

In our case, this triggered **multiple related bugs at once**:

- 33 hours of `WARNING gateway.platforms.telegram: [Telegram] Telegram polling conflict (1/3), will retry in 10s` repeated every 10s in container logs
- Container exited with code 255 after exhausting retries
- Native gateway drained within the same window because the user was effectively locked out from stopping the source of conflict
- Several already-open issues trace to this same root cause: #29325 (polling can conflict without visible duplicate gateway), #30122 / #30127 / #30130 / #40691 (related PTB network-retry-loop vs `_handle_polling_conflict` race)

If `enabled: false` in `config.yaml` actually disabled the platform, none of this would have happened — the container's `config.yaml` already correctly said `platforms.telegram.enabled: false`. The bot-token leak from `.env` would have stayed harmless.

## Reproduction (minimal)

1. Build any Hermes installation
2. Set `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=…` in `~/.hermes/.env`
3. Set in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:
   ```yaml
   platforms:
     telegram:
       enabled: false
   ```
4. Start the gateway
5. Observe the Telegram adapter polling `api.telegram.org` despite the explicit disable

Expected: gateway logs `No messaging platforms enabled.` or similar and does not open a Telegram connection.
Actual: Telegram adapter comes up and starts polling.

## Environment

- Hermes commit (container image): built `2026-06-18T20:54:16Z` from image `sha256:4b1d16b9…dfa`, predates `_enable_from_env` migration
- Hermes commit (local checkout with fix already present): HEAD includes commit `156176a44` ("fix: gateway log component + explicit-disable across migrated plugin platforms"), so `_enabled_explicit` machinery exists in tree but the Telegram `_apply_env_overrides` branch hasn't been migrated to use it
- Deployment: container alongside native install on the same WSL2 host

## Related

- #25065 — same pattern, Home Assistant
- #47804 — same pattern, Feishu
- #48820 — "Messaging gateway has 3 fragility bugs … env override ignores yaml" (Windows)
- #41112 — original PR that introduced the Slack fix (`_enable_from_env` + `_enabled_explicit`)
- Commit `156176a44` — `fix: gateway log component + explicit-disable across migrated plugin platforms` (generalized the fix; commit message specifically mentions telegram and matrix as targets for the marker)
- #29325 / #30122 / #30127 / #30130 / #40691 — 409 polling-conflict class of bugs that this fix would prevent by stopping the container from polling in the first place

items.title: Native Gemini: parallel tool calls emit consecutive same-role contents and 400 on the alternation check

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
### What happens

`_build_gemini_contents` in `agent/gemini_native_adapter.py` emits one `contents` entry per source message and never merges adjacent same-role entries. The native Gemini `generateContent` API requires strict user/model alternation and rejects consecutive same-role turns:

```
400 ... Please ensure that multiturn requests alternate between user and model.
```

Each tool result is translated into its own `{"role": "user", "parts": [functionResponse]}` entry. So when the model issues a parallel tool call (two or more tool calls in a single turn, which is a normal, default capability), the two tool results become two consecutive `user` contents, which Gemini rejects. Back-to-back user messages and merged assistant turns hit the same wall.

The sibling converters both merge: `convert_messages_to_anthropic` merges consecutive tool results into one user message, and `convert_messages_to_converse` appends a tool result to the preceding user turn. The native Gemini path has no equivalent.

### Reproduction

```python
from agent.gemini_native_adapter import _build_gemini_contents

messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Read a.txt and b.txt"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "", "tool_calls": [
        {"id": "call_1", "type": "function",
         "function": {"name": "read_file", "arguments": '{"path": "a.txt"}'}},
        {"id": "call_2", "type": "function",
         "function": {"name": "read_file", "arguments": '{"path": "b.txt"}'}},
    ]},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_1", "content": "AAA"},
    {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": "call_2", "content": "BBB"},
    {"role": "user", "content": "thanks"},
]

contents, _ = _build_gemini_contents(messages)
print([c["role"] for c in contents])
# ['user', 'model', 'user', 'user', 'user']
```

The three trailing `user` contents (two function responses plus the next user turn) are consecutive, so the request fails the alternation check.

### Impact

Any turn where the model calls more than one tool in parallel produces an unsendable history on the native Gemini provider. The request fails with a 400, and because the offending shape is now part of the stored conversation, the next turn rebuilds the same invalid contents and fails again. Parallel tool calling is a core, default capability, so this takes out multi-tool turns on native Gemini with no workaround short of disabling parallel calls.

### Fix

Merge adjacent same-role `contents` by concatenating their parts after the per-message loop. For a parallel call this yields the grouped multi-`functionResponse` user turn Gemini expects, and it fixes back-to-back user and assistant turns too.

items.body:
### Summary
With a non-loopback dashboard bind (`--host 0.0.0.0`) and the bundled **basic** username/password provider as the *only* registered auth provider, every unauthenticated HTML navigation returns **HTTP 500** instead of the login form. The dashboard is completely unreachable.

### Environment
- Hermes Agent v0.17.0 (upstream `ccc92c52`)
- `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0`, auth via `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_USERNAME` / `_PASSWORD` / `_SECRET`
- Only the `basic` provider registered (no Nous/OIDC)

### Root cause
`gated_auth_middleware` → `_auto_sso_response()` (`hermes_cli/dashboard_auth/middleware.py:140`) is an OAuth-only shortcut: when exactly one interactive provider is registered it 302-redirects to `/auth/login?provider=<name>` to skip the `/login` chooser. The `/auth/login` route (`hermes_cli/dashboard_auth/routes.py:197`) unconditionally calls `provider.start_login()`. The `basic` provider is password-only and raises:

```
NotImplementedError: BasicAuthProvider is password-only; there is no OAuth redirect flow. The login page POSTs to /auth/password-login instead.
```

→ unhandled → HTTP 500. The `/login` page and `/auth/password-login` flow are themselves correct; auto-SSO just routes *past* them into a flow the provider doesn't implement.

### Suggested fix
In `_auto_sso_response`, skip the SSO shortcut when the sole provider is password-based, so it falls through to the `/login` interstitial:

```python
provider = providers[0]
# Password-only providers have no OAuth redirect / start_login flow —
# auto-SSO to /auth/login would 500. Fall through to /login (form).
if getattr(provider, "supports_password", False):
    return None
```

### Repro
1. Set `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_USERNAME` / `HERMES_DASHBOARD_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD`
2. `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0`
3. Load `/` with no session cookie → 500 (expected: `/login` form)

items.title: Signal send crashes (UnicodeEncodeError) on a lone surrogate in a formatted reply

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
### What happens

`markdown_to_signal` in `gateway/platforms/signal_format.py` measures bodyRange offsets in UTF-16 code units:

```python
def _utf16_len(s: str) -> int:
    return len(s.encode("utf-16-le")) // 2
```

A lone surrogate code point (U+D800-U+DFFF) cannot be UTF-16 encoded, so `s.encode("utf-16-le")` raises `UnicodeEncodeError`. `_utf16_len` runs once per formatted span, so any reply that contains both a lone surrogate and a markdown span (bold, heading, inline code, italic) aborts the whole `SignalAdapter.send()` and the reply never reaches the user.

Lone surrogates do show up in model output. The codebase already sanitizes them with `_sanitize_surrogates` (the comment there cites "Kimi/GLM via Ollama can return invalid surrogate code points"), but that pass only cleans the copy stored in history. The text actually delivered is `final_response = assistant_message.content` (the raw SDK content, `agent/conversation_loop.py`), and the gateway delivery sanitizer (`_sanitize_gateway_final_response`) does not strip surrogates, so the raw surrogate reaches the Signal formatter.

### Reproduction

```python
from gateway.platforms.signal_format import markdown_to_signal

# a truncated-emoji half plus a normal bold span
markdown_to_signal("**bold \ud800 text**")
# UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-16-le' codec can't encode character '\ud800' ...
```

### Impact

When a model emits a lone surrogate (common with some local/Ollama-hosted backends) and the reply contains any markdown (almost every reply does), the Signal send crashes instead of delivering. The user gets no response, and the same stored response re-crashes on retry. Plain-text fallback does not help because the crash is in the formatting step that runs before the send.

### Fix

Replace lone surrogates with U+FFFD at the top of `markdown_to_signal`, before any UTF-16 offset math, mirroring the `_sanitize_surrogates` pass used elsewhere. A lone surrogate has no valid Signal representation anyway, so substituting the replacement character keeps the message deliverable.

items.title: [Bug]: STT configured plugin provider falls back to generic no-provider error when not registered
items.body:
## Summary

When `stt.provider` is set to a non-built-in STT backend name that is not registered as a command provider or plugin provider, `tools.transcription_tools.transcribe_audio()` falls through to the generic `No STT provider available` message.

That loses the configured provider name, so operators do not get told that `stt.provider='openrouter'` (or another custom/plugin id) is the value Hermes could not resolve. The image/video generation paths already surface this class of failure as `provider_not_registered` with a `hermes plugins list` hint.

## Environment / version

- Repository: `NousResearch/hermes-agent`
- Observed on upstream `main` at `f171842f0` on 2026-06-29
- Area: `tools/transcription_tools.py` STT plugin dispatch

## Reproduction

1. Enable STT.
2. Set `stt.provider: openrouter` (or another non-built-in provider id).
3. Do not install/register a matching transcription plugin, and do not define `stt.providers.openrouter.command`.
4. Trigger audio transcription, for example from a voice message path.

## Actual behavior

The configured provider is dropped from the final error and Hermes returns the generic setup guidance:

```text
No STT provider available. Install faster-whisper for free local transcription, configure HERMES_LOCAL_STT_COMMAND ...
```

## Expected behavior

Because the user explicitly configured a provider name, Hermes should return a provider-specific diagnostic such as:

```text
stt.provider='openrouter' is set but no built-in, command, or plugin provider registered that name. Run `hermes plugins list` ...
```

## Why this matters

The current error sends operators toward generic STT setup and credential checks instead of the real issue: a stale/missing plugin registration or missing command-provider declaration. This is the same class of diagnostic boundary as openclaw/openclaw#97484, where a missing media provider needed an actionable, capability-specific recovery hint.

## Scope boundary

This should not change:

- auto-detect failure when no explicit `stt.provider` is set
- built-in provider behavior such as `groq`, `openai`, `mistral`, `xai`, or `elevenlabs`
- command-provider precedence under `stt.providers.<name>`
- plugin availability errors when a matching plugin is registered but reports missing credentials/dependencies

items.title: Built-in TTS providers buffer unbounded upstream responses
items.body:
## Summary

Hermes' built-in xAI, MiniMax, and Gemini TTS providers read upstream response bodies without an explicit size cap. These paths call `requests.post()` with the default eager download behavior and then consume `response.content`, `response.json()`, or `response.text`, so a misconfigured or hostile endpoint can force the agent process to buffer an unexpectedly large audio or JSON response.

## Affected paths

- `tools/tts_tool.py::_generate_xai_tts` writes `response.content` after `POST /tts`.
- `tools/tts_tool.py::_generate_minimax_tts` parses t2a_v2 JSON and writes legacy raw audio from `response.content`.
- `tools/tts_tool.py::_generate_gemini_tts` parses success/error JSON and previews error text from the same unbounded response body.

## Why this matters

TTS is user-triggerable through voice/read-aloud workflows and supports configurable base URLs for some providers. A large success JSON body, hex/base64 audio payload, or raw audio response can be buffered before Hermes has a chance to reject it, increasing OOM/hang risk for long-running gateway/desktop processes.

## Expected behavior

Hermes should stream these TTS responses with a fixed byte limit, cancel/close the response once the limit is exceeded, and preserve normal behavior for small audio and JSON responses.

## Scope boundaries

This report is limited to built-in TTS response-body reads. It is not about text length caps, voice playback timeout behavior, or adding new audio endpoints.

_AI-assisted._

items.body:
# [Bug] MoA virtual provider auto-selects on "remove anthropic" without explicit /model moa command

## Summary
A TUI chat silently switches its runtime model to `moa` provider even though the user never typed a `/model moa:*` command and never explicitly invoked the moa aggregator. The system note that records the change reads:

> `[System: The active model for this chat has changed to default via provider moa. ...]`

After the (failed) moa switch, the user is told "from this point forward, use this runtime metadata when answering questions about what model/provider is active", but the model they actually want is their real default (`opencode-go / minimax-m3`).

## Reproduction

### Environment
- `Hermes Agent v0.17.0` (2026.6.19), upstream `929dd9c0`, local `68ca29db` (+31 carried commits)
- Profile: `default` (TUI)
- `~/.hermes/config.yaml` has the following `moa` block (both presets `enabled: false`, but the `moa:` block itself is present with `default_preset: ''` and `active_preset: ''`):

```yaml
moa:
  default_preset: ''
  active_preset: ''
  presets:
    default:
      enabled: false
      reference_models:
        - provider: kimi-coding
          model: kimi-k2.6
      aggregator:
        provider: kimi-coding
        model: kimi-k2.6
      reference_temperature: 0.6
      aggregator_temperature: 0.4
      max_tokens: 4096
    klo:
      enabled: false
      reference_models:
        - provider: openai-codex
          model: gpt-5.4
        - provider: kimi-coding
          model: kimi-k2.6
      aggregator:
        provider: kimi-coding
        model: kimi-k2.6
      reference_temperature: 0.6
      aggregator_temperature: 0.4
      max_tokens: 4096
  max_tokens: 4096
  enabled: true
```

### Steps
1. Start a TUI session on the real default: `opencode-go / minimax-m3`.
2. Send a chat message: `remove anthropic provider from model list of mine,`
3. The agent turns (reaches some code path that calls `ModelSwitchResult(success=True, target_provider="moa", new_model="default")`).
4. The next user turn receives the system-history pivot:
   ```
   [System: The active model for this chat has changed to default via provider moa. ...]
   ```
5. The chat is now pinned to `moa` and subsequent `/model` invocations report "does not work" because (a) `moa.default_preset` is empty, and (b) the moa aggregator credentials may not be configured for this profile — so any further `/model` call inside the same session lands on a broken provider.

## Expected
A free-form user message like "remove anthropic provider from model list" must NOT trigger an implicit `/model moa` switch. The active provider should stay on whatever the session default was (here: `opencode-go`). At most, the agent should call a `providers:` config-edit tool, not `switch_model()`.

## Actual
The active provider is rewritten to `moa` and recorded in the session's `model_override` dict. The TUI client receives a `session.info` event and a system-history marker telling the model "use moa from now on". The user never typed `/model`, never typed `moa:`, and the agent never asked for confirmation.

## Where in the code

The TUI gateway appends the marker at `tui_gateway/server.py:2731-2733`:

```python
_append_model_switch_marker(
    session, model=result.new_model, provider=result.target_provider
)
```

The `target_provider == "moa"` branch lives in `hermes_cli/model_switch.py:873-880` (PATH A: explicit provider) and `:965-973` (PATH B: no explicit provider, which calls `exact_moa_preset_name(_moa_cfg, raw_input)` and silently matches if `raw_input` is a key in `cfg["presets"]`):

```python
_moa_cfg = normalize_moa_config(load_config().get("moa") or {})
_moa_match = exact_moa_preset_name(_moa_cfg, raw_input)
if _moa_match:
    target_provider = "moa"
    new_model = _moa_match
```

`exact_moa_preset_name` in `hermes_cli/moa_config.py:160-167` does a literal string match:

```python
def exact_moa_preset_name(config: Any, text: str) -> str | None:
    wanted = str(text or "").strip()
    if not wanted:
        return None
    cfg = normalize_moa_config(config)
    return wanted if wanted in cfg["presets"] else None
```

Two suspicious things here:
1. `normalize_moa_config` keeps every preset in the dict regardless of `enabled: false`. The presence of any key in `presets:` is enough to be matched — `enabled: false` does not gate this. So a user who *intentionally* disabled their `default` moa preset to opt out is silently opted back in any time some code path passes `"default"` as the model name.
2. There is no caller-side guard that the agent actually issued an explicit `/model moa:<preset>` command. The LLM can drive `switch_model(new_model="default", new_provider=...)` indirectly via whatever model-picker or runtime path it is on, and the model_switch pipeline accepts it without checking that the model name came from a user-typed moa command. PATH A explicitly says "no explicit provider", but if the LLM passes `--provider moa` and `--model default`, the explicit branch is taken and the same moa pivot is performed.

## Suggested fix

- Make `exact_moa_preset_name` (or its caller) reject the match when the preset's `enabled: false`.
- In `hermes_cli/model_switch.py:965-973`, require that the `raw_input` literally started with `moa:` to take the moa branch — do not allow any other code path to land on `target_provider = "moa"` silently. The "early MoA preset syntax" at line 821 already enforces this for the `moa:foo` form, but PATH B at 965 has no such guard.
- In `tui_gateway/server.py:2731`, before calling `_append_model_switch_marker`, emit a confirmation event to the TUI client when the new provider differs from `current_provider` and the change did not originate from a user-typed `/model` command (i.e. the LLM asked for it). Confirm or roll back.

## Workaround

Set `moa.enabled: false` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` so the `moa:` block never gets selected. Editing this from inside the agent is blocked by Hermes' config-write guard, so the user has to edit the file by hand. After the fix lands this workaround should not be necessary.

## Related

- `feat(moa): make /moa one-shot only; route preset switching through the model picker` — `50f685521` (recent change to moa routing that may have introduced this regression)
- The `model_switch` module's `resolved_moa_preset` flag at `hermes_cli/model_switch.py:815` is set in PATH A (line 830) and PATH B (line 973) but never read by the gateway to gate the marker append.

items.title: Desktop (macOS): renderer crash-loops to frozen window when a conversation reaches the ~128K-token compaction threshold
items.body:
## Summary
On macOS, Hermes Desktop's Electron **renderer** repeatedly crashes (and is then
reload-suppressed into a frozen/blank window) when the active conversation grows
to the context-compaction threshold (~128K tokens). The backend stays healthy
throughout — only the window process dies.

## Environment
- macOS (Apple Silicon, arm64)
- Hermes Desktop 0.17.0 (renderer build 309)
- Backend (`serve` + gateway): healthy the entire time

## Symptoms
The renderer crashes ~every 20s, identically, then Hermes gives up:
```
[renderer] render-process-gone reason=crashed exitCode=5   (x4)
[renderer] suppressing reload: 3 crashes within 60000ms (likely a crash loop)
```
After suppression the window is frozen/blank. The Python backend keeps accepting
WebSocket connections the whole time.

## Trigger (consistent across both crash loops in the log)
Immediately before each loop:
```
Preflight compression: ~128,995 tokens >= 128,000 threshold. This may take a moment.
Compacting context — summarizing earlier conversation so I can continue...
Interrupted during API call.
[renderer] render-process-gone ...
```
The renderer appears to die rendering the full oversized conversation; on reload
it re-renders the same conversation and crashes again. The backend compaction
that would shrink the session keeps getting interrupted by the crash, so the
session never gets smaller on its own.

## Crash signature (6 identical reports, 16:53–16:55)
- `EXC_BREAKPOINT (SIGTRAP)`, exitCode 5, on thread `CrRendererMain`
- Stack inside V8 garbage collection (`v8::CppHeap::CollectGarbage...`, `cppgc::...`)
- All six reports hit the same address — deterministic, not random instability
- System RAM was ~50% free at crash time, so this is not machine-wide memory pressure

Reports: `~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/Hermes Helper (Renderer)-*.ips`

## Expected
A large conversation should render without crashing the renderer (virtualize /
paginate long histories; cap renderer heap usage), and compaction should be able
to complete instead of being killed by a renderer crash loop.

## Workaround
After restart, don't reopen the oversized conversation (start a new chat / switch
sessions first), or the loop re-triggers.

## Possibly related
- #44785 (renderer crash rendering oversized message content — image-upload path)
- #43242 (macOS renderer OOM, but at startup / different mechanism)

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main

labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

In gateway mode (including the Desktop GUI), terminal tool subprocesses cannot reliably determine which session they are executing in. Both `HERMES_SESSION_KEY` and `HERMES_SESSION_ID` environment variables are either absent or stale in `os.environ`, making it impossible for tools (especially `terminal`) to know the current session ID.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Launch Hermes Desktop GUI (gateway mode, `HERMES_DESKTOP=1`)
2. Open multiple sessions (e.g., session A and session B)
3. In session A, run `echo $HERMES_SESSION_KEY` and `echo $HERMES_SESSION_ID` via the `terminal` tool
4. Compare the output with the actual session ID (from `hermes sessions list` or the UI)

## Observed Behavior

```
$ echo $HERMES_SESSION_KEY
20260630_042152_952357          # This is a GATEWAY session key, not the current session ID

$ echo $HERMES_SESSION_ID
20260630_042954_cee564          # Also wrong; actual current session is 20260630_042754_2b07dc
```

Neither value matches the actual current session ID (`20260630_042754_2b07dc`).

## Root Cause Analysis

Two design decisions combine to create this gap:

### 1. `HERMES_SESSION_KEY` is deliberately excluded from `os.environ` in gateway mode

From `gateway/run.py` L15889:
```python
# We deliberately do NOT write os.environ["HERMES_SESSION_KEY"] here:
# os.environ is process-global, so concurrent gateway sessions (e.g.
# two Discord threads) would clobber each other's value...
```

This is correct for concurrency safety — but it means terminal subprocesses (which inherit `os.environ`) cannot read it.

### 2. `HERMES_SESSION_ID` may be stale or unset

`set_current_session_id()` in `gateway/session_context.py` does write to both ContextVar and `os.environ`. However, in the Desktop/TUI code path, this function may not be called with the correct session ID, or the `os.environ` value may be from a previous session initialization.

### 3. Terminal subprocesses rely entirely on `os.environ`

The `terminal` tool spawns a shell subprocess that inherits `os.environ`. Since neither `HERMES_SESSION_KEY` nor `HERMES_SESSION_ID` reflects the current session, tools have no way to determine their execution context.

## Impact

- **Plugins and tools** that need to know the current session ID (e.g., for logging, session-specific behavior, or cross-referencing) cannot do so reliably
- **`session_search` workaround**: Agents can query `state.db` to find the most recent session, but this is fragile (edge cases with concurrent sessions, and the current message is not in the DB yet)
- **No known reliable method** exists for a tool to determine which session it is executing in when running in gateway/Desktop mode

## Suggested Fix

Options (from least to most invasive):

1. **Pass session ID as a process argument**: When the `terminal` tool spawns a subprocess, pass the current session ID via `--session-id` CLI argument (similar to how the TUI slash-worker already does this for `HERMES_SESSION_KEY`). The subprocess can then export it.

2. **Write session ID to a per-session file**: Create a temporary file (e.g., `/tmp/hermes-session-{pid}`) containing the session ID before spawning the subprocess, and clean it up after.

3. **Use a ContextVar-aware mechanism**: Since `os.environ` is process-global and can not safely hold per-session values, consider a mechanism where the tool worker thread reads the ContextVar directly (it already inherits ContextVars from the parent thread in Python).

Option 3 seems most natural — Python ContextVars are inherited by child threads, so the tool worker thread should already have access to the correct value via `_SESSION_KEY` and `_SESSION_ID`. The issue is that the `terminal` tool spawns a subprocess, not a thread, so ContextVars do not propagate.

## Environment

- Hermes Desktop GUI (`HERMES_DESKTOP=1`)
- Windows (git-bash shell)
- Hermes Agent version: latest (2026-06-30)
- Gateway mode (`HERMES_GATEWAY_SESSION=1`)
- Profile: lotusy

## Related

- #37356 (delegate_task subagent overwrites `HERMES_SESSION_ID`) — related but different root cause
- #24100 (referenced in source code comment about session key clobbering)

## Problem

`plugins/platforms/discord/adapter.py::_standalone_send` talks to the Discord REST API directly when Hermes needs to send Discord messages without a live gateway adapter, for example standalone `send_message_tool` / cron delivery paths.

Several response reads in that path currently use unbounded aiohttp helpers:

- forum/thread creation success path: `await resp.json()`
- ordinary message/media success path: `await resp.json()`
- Discord API error paths: `await resp.text()`

The standalone Discord sender should bound success JSON reads and error-body snippets before parsing/formatting them. The cap should be local to this REST fallback path and preserve existing behavior for normal Discord responses.

## Notes

This is the same boundary class as recent OpenClaw response-body cap fixes, but the Hermes surface is different: Hermes does not have the exact PluralKit / Discord voice upload URL calls. The matching Hermes surface is its standalone Discord REST sender.

items.body:
## Summary

Deleting a credential from the credential pool via the dashboard (System Settings → Credentials → Remove) shows a success toast "Credential removed", but the entry **reappears on page refresh**. The credential is never actually gone.

## Root Cause

The dashboard DELETE endpoint (`DELETE /api/credentials/pool/{provider}/{index}` in `web_server.py`) calls `pool.remove_index(index)`, which correctly removes the entry from `auth.json` via `write_credential_pool()`.

However, `load_pool()` is called on the **next** GET (e.g. when refreshing the dashboard), and it calls `_seed_from_env()` and `_seed_from_singletons()` — which **re-create** the pool entry from the matching environment variable or auth file. Since the API key is still in `.env`, the entry comes right back.

The CLI `hermes auth remove` command handles this correctly by calling `suppress_credential_source(provider, removed.source)` after removal (`auth_commands.py:475`). This marks the source as suppressed so the seeding functions skip it.

The dashboard endpoint is **missing this call**.

## Reproduction

1. Open dashboard → System Settings → Credentials
2. Delete any credential (e.g. `xiaomi`)
3. Toast: "Credential removed" ✅
4. Refresh the page
5. The credential is back ❌

## Fix

Add `suppress_credential_source(provider, removed.source)` to the DELETE handler after successful removal, matching the CLI behavior:

```python
if removed.source:
    from hermes_cli.auth import suppress_credential_source
    suppress_credential_source(provider, removed.source)
```

PR incoming.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.17.0 (`f171842f`), current `main`

items.body:
## Problem

`/v1/responses` supports OpenAI-style `previous_response_id` chaining and a `truncation: auto` request option. When a stored response history is longer than 100 messages, the handler currently keeps only `conversation_history[-100:]`.

That drops Hermes' leading context-compaction handoff message, e.g. `[CONTEXT COMPACTION — REFERENCE ONLY] ...`, when the session has already been compacted. The next agent turn then keeps the recent tail but loses the summary that preserved all pre-compaction context.

## Why it matters

Responses API clients that use `previous_response_id` plus `truncation: auto` can silently lose continuity after context compression. The request still succeeds, but the model no longer receives the compacted-history handoff that explains earlier turns.

## Reproduction

A minimal synthetic reproduction uses the API server response store:

1. Store a previous response with `conversation_history` containing one leading compaction summary followed by 149 normal messages.
2. POST `/v1/responses` with:
   - `previous_response_id` pointing at that stored response
   - `truncation: auto`
   - a new `input` value
3. Inspect the `conversation_history` passed to `_run_agent`.

## Actual behavior

The handler passes the last 100 messages only. The leading compaction summary is omitted.

## Expected behavior

`truncation: auto` should still cap the history at 100 messages, but preserve leading compaction summary/handoff messages and fill the remainder with the most recent conversation tail.

## Scope

This is limited to the OpenAI-compatible API server `/v1/responses` path. It does not change normal chat completions, session DB storage, compression itself, or non-auto truncation behavior.

items.title: Add config flag to disable trigram FTS index (prevent state.db bloat)

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Problem

The `messages_fts_trigram` FTS5 index grows disproportionately large relative to the message data it indexes. On a production headless gateway with ~100K messages spanning ~65 days:

**Sizes measured via `dbstat`:**

| Component | Size |
|---|---|
| `messages_fts_trigram_data` | 2,147 MB |
| `messages_fts_trigram_content` | 670 MB |
| `messages_fts_trigram_idx` | 1 MB |
| **Total trigram** | **~2.8 GB** |
| `messages` table | 795 MB |
| `messages_fts` (standard) | ~1 GB |
| `sessions` | 125 MB |
| **Total `state.db`** | **5.9 GB** (pre-prune) |

The trigram tokenizer indexes every 3-character window, so large repeated content — such as operator/system prompts in the 275 KB range injected per cron-driven message — inflates the index disproportionately. This is compounded by the `_content` shadow table duplicating message text that already exists in `messages`.

In practice, `state.db` reached 5.9 GB within 2 months of operation, causing `hermes update`'s pre-update backup (which zips the entire DB) to hang indefinitely during the zip operation. Three consecutive update attempts stalled at the backup stage until the backup was skipped with `--no-backup`.

## Impact

- `state.db` bloats to multiple GB within weeks on active headless gateways
- Pre-update backup hangs or consumes excessive time/memory
- The trigram index provides substring/fuzzy/CJK matching that a headless gateway deployment rarely exercises — standard `messages_fts` covers the token/word search path that `search_messages()` uses by default

## Current behavior

`hermes_state.py` unconditionally creates `messages_fts_trigram` via `_ensure_fts_schema()` during schema init (~line 1463). `CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` means even if an admin manually drops the table, Hermes recreates it (and its triggers) on next gateway restart.

## Proposed solution

Add a config flag under a grouped `fts` namespace so future FTS-related options have a home:

```yaml
state_db:
  fts:
    trigram: true  # default: true (preserves current behavior)
```

When `false`:
1. Skip `CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE messages_fts_trigram` and its triggers in `_ensure_fts_schema`
2. Set `self._trigram_available = False` so `search_messages()` skips the trigram code path

**Default preserves current behavior** — no change for existing users unless they opt in.

**Migration / reclamation:** For already-bloated databases, dropping trigram + `VACUUM` reclaims the space immediately (`DROP TABLE messages_fts_trigram; VACUUM;`). The index is fully rebuildable from `messages` if trigram is re-enabled later.

**Search impact:** Normal word/token queries still use standard `messages_fts` at full quality. Only substring and CJK queries that previously hit the trigram path degrade to `LIKE`. I'd appreciate maintainer input on which features (if any) depend on trigram matching beyond `search_messages()`.

## Alternatives considered

- **Automated message pruning (30-day retention):** Reduces growth rate but doesn't address the trigram amplifier — the index is still disproportionately large relative to retained data.
- **External-content FTS (`content='messages'`):** Would eliminate the `_content` shadow table duplication (~670 MB saved). Separate optimization; happy to file as a follow-up issue if there's interest.
- **Manual `DROP TABLE` without config flag:** Works until next gateway restart recreates the table. Not durable across updates or restarts.

## Workaround in use

Patching `hermes_state.py` to check an `HERMES_FTS_TRIGRAM_DISABLE` env var in the schema init path. Functional but requires reapplication after every `hermes update`.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.17.0
- Linux (Hetzner, 16 GB RAM)
- Headless gateway: Telegram + cron-driven agent sessions, ~100K messages over 65 days

Happy to submit a PR implementing the config flag if there's interest.

items.title: Signal RPC reads unbounded response bodies
items.body:
### Summary

`SignalAdapter._rpc()` reads the full signal-cli-rest-api JSON response into memory before parsing it. A misconfigured, buggy, or hostile Signal bridge can return an oversized JSON body or error body and force Hermes to buffer it inside the gateway process.

This is the same failure class recently fixed in OpenClaw's Signal container REST client in openclaw/openclaw#97539: container-local Signal REST APIs are trusted operationally, but they are still HTTP peers and should not be allowed to provide unbounded response bodies.

### Affected path

- `gateway/platforms/signal.py`
- `SignalAdapter._rpc()`
- Any Signal operation that calls `/api/v1/rpc`, including sends, attachment fetches, contact lookups, reactions, and typing-related RPCs.

### Actual behavior

The RPC helper calls the client request and then parses the response body as JSON without enforcing a byte limit. That means the response body can grow until the Python/httpx buffer or process memory is exhausted.

### Expected behavior

Signal RPC responses should be read with a bounded maximum size. Oversized responses should fail the RPC cleanly and log the failure, without changing the successful JSON-RPC result/error behavior for normal signal-cli-rest-api responses.

### Notes

This is not a secret exposure issue. It is an availability hardening issue for a locally configured HTTP bridge.

items.title: Slack stale thread sessions suppress reset-time thread context

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

Slack thread replies can skip the first-turn thread-history reseed after the existing Hermes session has gone stale under the configured reset policy.

`SlackAdapter._has_active_session_for_thread()` currently treats a thread as active when the computed session key exists in `SessionStore._entries`. That check does not ask the session store whether the entry would be reset by the daily/idle/suspended reset policy. The real message path later calls `get_or_create_session()`, which can roll the same session key to a fresh session id.

## Impact

When a Slack thread has prior conversation history and the Hermes session expires, the next reply in that thread can be routed as if the old session is still active. Because `_fetch_thread_context()` is guarded by `not _has_active_session_for_thread(...)`, Hermes does not prepend recent Slack thread history on the first turn of the fresh session.

The model then receives the new reply without the thread context the operator expects after reset.

## Reproduction outline

1. Configure Slack with thread replies and a reset policy such as `idle`/`both` with a short idle window.
2. Start a Slack thread that creates a Hermes session entry for `(channel_id, thread_ts)`.
3. Let that entry pass the reset boundary.
4. Send a new reply in the same Slack thread.

Expected: the first turn after reset should be treated as a cold/stale thread session and should fetch the configured Slack thread context.

Actual: `_has_active_session_for_thread()` returns true because the key is present in `_entries`, suppressing the thread-context fetch before `get_or_create_session()` performs the reset.

## Notes

This is the same bug shape as the recent OpenClaw Slack reset-context fix: the platform-specific thread active check must share the session store freshness boundary, not just test key presence.

items.title: [Bug] Cron delivery to private chat forum-topics lands in General — direct_messages_topic_id silently ignored (regression from #50023)

items.body:
## Summary

PR #50023 (fixing #22773) routes all Telegram private-chat cron deliveries through `direct_messages_topic_id` instead of `message_thread_id`. However, `direct_messages_topic_id` is **silently ignored** by Telegram for private chats that use **forum-style topics** (created via `createForumTopic` API). Messages land in General with `ok: true` — no error, no warning.

This is a different chat topology than the original #22773 issue: those users had Telegram's native "Direct Messages topics" mode (where `message_thread_id` was rejected with 400). Our chat uses standard forum topics in a private chat, where `message_thread_id` works correctly and `direct_messages_topic_id` is silently dropped.

The Telegram server-side regression that caused #22022 / #22773 was [fixed by Telegram on May 9, 2026](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/79455#resolution). `message_thread_id` now works for all private-chat topic types. Using `direct_messages_topic_id` as a blanket replacement causes a silent regression for forum-topic private chats.

## Reproduction

1. **Chat type:** Private chat (`getChat` returns `type: private`, no `is_forum` field)
2. **Topics:** Created via Bot API `createForumTopic` — returns numeric `message_thread_id`
3. **Hermes config:** `telegram.extra.dm_topics` with `thread_id` values
4. **Cron job:** `deliver: telegram:<chat_id>:<thread_id>`
5. Gateway is **running** → cron delivers via live adapter path → `scheduler.py:1251-1266` classifies as `is_private_dm_topic` → uses `direct_messages_topic_id` → **message lands in General**

### Raw Bot API evidence

```bash
# message_thread_id → CORRECT (lands in topic)
curl sendMessage -d '{"chat_id": 978174799, "message_thread_id": 252345, "text": "test"}'
# Response: ok: true, message_thread_id: 252345, is_topic_message: true

# direct_messages_topic_id → WRONG (lands in General, silently ignored)
curl sendMessage -d '{"chat_id": 978174799, "direct_messages_topic_id": 252345, "text": "test"}'
# Response: ok: true, message_thread_id: null, is_topic_message: null  ← no error, wrong location!
```

The user confirmed via Telegram: `message_thread_id` messages appear in the correct topic; `direct_messages_topic_id` messages appear in General/All Messages.

## Root Cause

`cron/scheduler.py:1251-1266`:

```python
is_private_dm_topic = (
    platform == Platform.TELEGRAM
    and thread_id is not None
    and _looks_like_telegram_private_chat_id(str(chat_id))  # chat_id > 0
    and _looks_like_int(str(thread_id))                      # numeric thread_id
)
if is_private_dm_topic:
    route_metadata = {"direct_messages_topic_id": str(thread_id), ...}
```

This assumes **all** positive chat_id + numeric thread_id = Bot API "Direct Messages" mode. But there are at least two distinct private-chat topic topologies:

| Topology | `message_thread_id` | `direct_messages_topic_id` | How created |
|----------|---------------------|---------------------------|-------------|
| Forum topics in private chat | ✅ Works | ❌ Silently ignored | `createForumTopic` API |
| Native "DM topics" mode | ❌ 400 error (pre-May 9 fix) | ✅ Works | Telegram client UI |

The code cannot distinguish between them, and uses the parameter that's wrong for the first (more common) case.

## Interesting observation: standalone path works

When the gateway is **down** during cron execution, the standalone fallback path (`_send_telegram` in `send_message_tool.py`) uses `message_thread_id` directly — and **delivery succeeds** in the correct topic. The bug only manifests when the live adapter path is used (gateway running).

## Suggested Fix

**Option A (preferred):** Use `message_thread_id` for all private-chat deliveries, with a fallback retry on `400 thread not found` → `direct_messages_topic_id`. This mirrors how the gateway adapter (`plugins/platforms/telegram/adapter.py`) already handles it and is resilient to both topologies.

**Option B:** Try `message_thread_id` first. On `400 Bad Request: message thread not found`, retry with `direct_messages_topic_id`.

Either way, **don't blanket-replace `message_thread_id` with `direct_messages_topic_id`** — the silent failure (ok: true, wrong location) is worse than a loud failure (400 error with retry).

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.17.0 (2026.6.19)
- Upstream commit: d2ce2c85
- Chat type: `private` with forum topics (not native DM topics mode)
- 4 DM topics configured in `telegram.extra.dm_topics`
- Platform: Telegram polling mode

## Related

- #22773 — original issue (cron → General), fixed by #50023 which introduced this regression
- #22022 — Bot API 10.0 broke `message_thread_id` (server-side, fixed by Telegram May 9)
- #21981 — earlier duplicate of #22022
- [openclaw/openclaw#79455](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/79455) — same root cause, same timeline, Telegram fixed server-side

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Summary

A Mixture-of-Agents turn fails on the aggregator step with `HTTP 404` when the aggregator's provider speaks the Anthropic Messages protocol but its endpoint host isn't one the URL heuristic recognizes. The reference models run fine and return their drafts, then the aggregator call dies:

```
API call failed after 3 retries: HTTP 404: Error code: 404
```

Logs show the failing call going out as `provider=moa model=<preset> base_url=moa://local`, and the underlying client built for the aggregator is a plain OpenAI client hitting `/chat/completions` against an endpoint that only serves `/v1/messages`.

## Environment

- MoA aggregator slot points at a custom provider whose endpoint uses the Anthropic Messages wire format (`api_mode: anthropic_messages`), hosted on a domain that is **not** `api.anthropic.com`, not a `*/anthropic` path, and not Kimi's `/coding` route.
- The same model works fine as the normal (non-MoA) main model, because the main turn resolves and applies `api_mode` correctly.

## Root cause

`agent/moa_loop.py::_slot_runtime` resolves each slot through `resolve_runtime_provider`, which returns `provider`, `base_url`, `api_key`, **and** `api_mode`. The function forwards `base_url` and `api_key` but drops `api_mode`.

Its own docstring says the resolved runtime is passed through "so the slot gets its provider's real API surface (anthropic_messages, max_completion_tokens, ...)", but `api_mode` never leaves the function. A code comment claims `call_llm` re-derives the transport from `base_url`. It can't:

- `call_llm` in `agent/auxiliary_client.py` has no `api_mode` parameter, so the caller can't pass it.
- The only fallback is the URL heuristic `_endpoint_speaks_anthropic_messages`, which matches `api.anthropic.com`, paths ending in `/anthropic`, and `api.kimi.com/coding`. Any other Anthropic-compatible host fails the check.

So the aggregator client is built for OpenAI `chat.completions`, the endpoint only answers `/v1/messages`, and the request 404s. The retry loop just repeats the same wrong request three times.

## Why the reference slot still works

The reference models in the failing setup happen to resolve to an OpenAI-wire endpoint, so dropping `api_mode` is harmless for them. The bug only bites a slot whose correct transport is Anthropic Messages on an unrecognized host. The aggregator is the most likely place to hit it since it's commonly a Claude-family model.

## Suggested fix

Forward the resolved `api_mode` from `_slot_runtime`, and give `call_llm` an optional `api_mode` parameter that overrides the auto-derived value. Both the aggregator and the reference path share `_slot_runtime`, so both get correct transport. Defaulting the new parameter to `None` keeps existing behavior unchanged for every current caller.

I've opened a PR with this fix plus regression tests.

## Version info

- Hermes Agent: v0.17.0 (2026.6.19)
- Python: 3.11.13
- OS: Linux (Rocky Linux 8.10, kernel 4.18)
- OpenAI SDK: 2.24.0

items.title: Hermes Agent gateway on ZFS corrupts state.db with multiple connections

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
# SQLite WAL Disk I/O Error on ZFS — Incident Report

**Date:** 2026-06-30  
**Reporter:** Hermes Agent user (TrueNAS / ZFS deployment)  
**Component:** `hermes_state.py` → `apply_wal_with_fallback()`  
**Severity:** Session-breaking — all session list / sidebar queries fail with "internal server error"  

---

## Summary

When running the Hermes Agent gateway on a **ZFS filesystem** (TrueNAS pool, `zfs rw,noatime,xattr,nfs4acl`), a rapid reconnect storm from a desktop client caused SQLite WAL shared-memory (SHM) corruption. Every subsequent `SessionDB()` connection failed with `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at `hermes_state.py:279`, rendering the session sidebar and `/api/sessions` endpoint non-functional until a full gateway restart.

---

## Environment

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Host OS | Linux (TrueNAS SCALE) |
| Filesystem | **ZFS** (`FastBits/FastStore` pool, mounted at `/opt/data`) |
| Mount options | `rw,noatime,xattr,nfs4acl,caseinsensitive` |
| Hermes state.db path | `/opt/data/state.db` (SQLite + WAL mode) |
| state.db size | ~3.4 MB |
| Disk space | 267 GB free (not a capacity issue) |

---

## Timeline of Events (2026-06-29)

All times are from server-local logs (`/opt/data/logs/errors.log`, `gui.log`).

| Time (local) | Event |
|---|---|
| **16:43:31.357** | 🔴 **First error.** `GET /api/sessions` fails — `SessionDB()` → `_connect_and_init()` → `apply_wal_with_fallback()` → `conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")` raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. |
| 16:43:31.396 | Second `GET /api/sessions` fails with the same error (sidebar retry). |
| 16:43:41.426 | WebUI WebSocket (`127.0.0.1:59492`) disconnects — `client_disconnect(code=1005)`. |
| 16:43:41.460 | Desktop client (`192.168.0.110:23005`) establishes new WebSocket connection. |
| 16:43:41.819 – 16:43:49.149 | **~25 rapid PTY connection attempts** from `192.168.0.110`, each ~350ms apart — a reconnect storm from the desktop client. Each connection spawns a new `SessionDB()` instance against the same `state.db`. |
| 16:43:49.550 | Third `GET /api/sessions` fails — same disk I/O error. The database connection is now fully wedged. |
| 16:44 onwards | All subsequent `SessionDB()` instantiations fail identically. Error repeats for the rest of the session. |
| ~07:27 (next day) | Gateway restarted; stale `state.db-wal` (0 bytes) and `state.db-shm` (32 KB) files cleaned/reinitialized by SQLite on fresh connection. Issue resolved. |

---

## Root Cause Analysis

### The trigger: Desktop client reconnect storm

The desktop client (connecting from `192.168.0.110`) entered a rapid reconnect loop, spawning approximately **25 new WebSocket/PTY connections within 8 seconds**. Each connection causes the gateway to open a new `SessionDB()` against `state.db`, which calls:

```python
# hermes_state.py, line 821 → 816 → 279
def _connect_and_init(self):
    ...
    apply_wal_with_fallback(self._conn, db_label="state.db")

# apply_wal_with_fallback, line 279
conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
```

This burst of concurrent WAL-mode connections on ZFS appears to have corrupted the WAL shared-memory file (`state.db-shm`).

### Why ZFS is the differentiator

SQLite's WAL mode uses a **shared-memory (mmap) file** (`-shm`) to coordinate between connections. On standard filesystems (ext4, XFS), mmap-based shared memory works reliably. On ZFS:

- ZFS does not support `mmap()` with `MAP_SHARED` for SQLite's `-shm` file in the same way ext4 does, because ZFS is a copy-on-write filesystem with different semantics for memory-mapped files.
- Under a burst of concurrent connections, the SHM file can enter an inconsistent state where all subsequent `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` calls fail with `disk I/O error` (not `locking protocol` — which is the NFS-style error the fallback code expects).
- The `apply_wal_with_fallback()` function checks for `_WAL_INCOMPAT_MARKERS` (like "locking protocol") to decide whether to fall back to `journal_mode=DELETE`. The error "disk I/O error" does **not** match these markers, so the exception is **re-raised** rather than gracefully degraded.

### Post-corruption state

After the initial corruption:
- `state.db-wal`: 0 bytes (empty/stale)
- `state.db-shm`: 32,768 bytes (wedged in inconsistent state)
- `state.db` main file: intact (data was not lost)
- Every new `SessionDB()` connection fails at `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` with `disk I/O error`
- The error persists until the gateway process is restarted, which releases file handles and allows SQLite to reinitialize the WAL/SHM files cleanly

---

## Code Path

```
SessionDB.__init__()                          # hermes_state.py:821
  └─ _connect_and_init()                      # hermes_state.py:816
       └─ apply_wal_with_fallback(            # hermes_state.py:248
              self._conn,
              db_label="state.db")
            └─ conn.execute(                 # hermes_state.py:279
                 "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
               → sqlite3.OperationalError:
                   disk I/O error  ← RAISED (no fallback)
```

The fallback logic at line 281–292 checks:
```python
except sqlite3.OperationalError as exc:
    msg = str(exc).lower()
    if not any(marker in msg for marker in _WAL_INCOMPATIBLE_MARKERS):
        raise  # ← This path is taken; "disk I/O error" is not in _WAL_INCOMPATIBLE_MARKERS
```

On ZFS, the error message is "disk I/O error" — not the expected "locking protocol" — so the fallback to `journal_mode=DELETE` never fires, and the exception propagates up to the web server's `/api/sessions` handler, which surfaces as the "internal server error" in the UI.

---

## Reproduction

**Confirmed trigger:** A desktop client reconnect storm (rapid WebSocket connect/disconnect cycle) while the gateway is running on ZFS.

**Conditions:**
1. Hermes Agent gateway running on ZFS filesystem
2. Dashboard/web server enabled (`hermes dashboard`)
3. A desktop client connecting to the gateway
4. The desktop client enters a rapid reconnect loop (can happen on network blip, sleep/wake, or client crash)

**Not required:** The corruption does not require disk space issues, permission problems, or a specific SQLite version — it is triggered by the concurrent-connection burst pattern on ZFS's mmap implementation.

---

## Proposed Mitigations

The following are suggested areas for investigation by the Hermes Agent development team:

### 1. Add "disk I/O error" to WAL fallback markers

The most direct fix: include `"disk i/o error"` (and potentially other generic SQLite I/O errors) in `_WAL_INCOMPATIBLE_MARKERS` so that `apply_wal_with_fallback()` gracefully falls back to `journal_mode=DELETE` on ZFS, just as it does on NFS/SMB/FUSE:

```python
# Suggested addition to _WAL_INCOMPATIBLE_MARKERS
_WAL_INCOMPATIBLE_MARKERS = (
    "locking protocol",
    "disk i/o error",   # ← ZFS SHM corruption presents as this
    ...
)
```

This would prevent the error from propagating and allow the session store to continue operating (in slower DELETE journal mode) instead of failing entirely.

### 2. Connection pooling / reuse

The reconnect storm caused ~25 rapid `SessionDB()` instantiations, each opening a fresh SQLite connection. A connection pool or cached singleton connection would reduce the number of concurrent WAL initializations and reduce the surface area for SHM corruption.

### 3. SHM corruption recovery

If `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` fails with a disk I/O error, consider automatically attempting to:
1. Close all connections to the database
2. Delete the `-wal` and `-shm` sidecar files
3. Reopen the connection and retry

This mirrors the manual recovery steps that resolved the issue (gateway restart → clean WAL/SHM reinitialization).

### 4. Reconnect storm throttling

The desktop client's rapid reconnect loop (~25 connections in 8 seconds) amplified what might otherwise have been a transient issue. A server-side rate limit on new WebSocket/PTY connections from the same client (e.g., max 3 new connections per 5 seconds, with exponential backoff) would prevent the burst pattern that triggers the corruption.

### 5. ZFS detection and proactive DELETE journal mode

Detect ZFS filesystem at startup (via `stat -f` or `/proc/mounts`) and proactively set `journal_mode=DELETE` instead of attempting WAL, similar to how the NFS fallback already works. This would eliminate the ZFS-specific failure mode entirely at the cost of reduced write concurrency.

---

## Conclusion

The incident was caused by the intersection of:
1. A desktop client reconnect storm (rapid connection churn)
2. ZFS's handling of SQLite WAL shared-memory files
3. The `apply_wal_with_fallback` function not recognizing "disk I/O error" as a WAL-incompatible marker

The gateway restart cleared the corrupted SHM state. The data in `state.db` was not affected — only the WAL coordination layer was wedged. The proposed mitigations above would prevent recurrence and improve resilience on ZFS deployments.

items.title: Lone surrogate in a reply crashes Telegram delivery: the delivered response is not surrogate-sanitized

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
### What happens

The model's reply is delivered as `final_response = assistant_message.content` (`agent/conversation_loop.py`), the raw SDK content. The gateway delivery boundary `_sanitize_gateway_final_response` (`gateway/run.py`) redacts secrets and classifies provider errors, but it does not strip lone surrogate code points. So a lone surrogate (U+D800-U+DFFF) in the reply reaches the chat-surface formatters unchanged.

On Telegram, every reply is measured by `utf16_len` (`gateway/platforms/base.py`), which does `s.encode("utf-16-le")`. A lone surrogate cannot be UTF-16 encoded, so the length check `if utf16_len(content) > self.MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH` (`plugins/platforms/telegram/adapter.py`) raises `UnicodeEncodeError` and the send aborts. The check runs on every reply, before any splitting, so even a short reply fails.

Lone surrogates do occur in model output. The codebase already sanitizes them with `_sanitize_surrogates` (the comment there cites "Kimi/GLM via Ollama can return invalid surrogate code points"), but that pass only cleans the copy stored in history via `build_assistant_message`. The delivered copy is never sanitized.

### Reproduction

```python
from gateway.platforms.base import utf16_len

# raw model reply containing a truncated-emoji half
content = "Here is your answer \ud800 done"
utf16_len(content)
# UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-16-le' codec can't encode character '\ud800' ...
```

This is the value `_sanitize_gateway_final_response` returns unchanged today, so it reaches the Telegram length check and crashes there.

### Impact

When a model emits a lone surrogate, the Telegram reply fails to deliver and the same stored response re-crashes on retry. This is distinct from #11467 (which fixed `truncate_message` slicing a *valid* surrogate pair into a lone half); here the lone surrogate is already present in the model output and crashes the length check before any slicing. It is the same class of gap that #55143 fixed inside the Signal formatter, but it is unaddressed for Telegram and any other chat surface, because the delivered text is not sanitized at the boundary they all pass through.

### Fix

Replace lone surrogates with U+FFFD in `_sanitize_gateway_final_response` for chat surfaces, mirroring the `_sanitize_surrogates` pass already applied to stored history. Raw-text/programmatic surfaces keep the existing passthrough (their JSON/file consumers escape surrogates).

items.body:
## Summary

Slack slash-command replies use the saved `response_url` to replace the initial ephemeral acknowledgement. When that POST returns a non-200 status, the adapter currently reads the full response body with `await resp.text()` before logging only a short prefix.

## Reproduction

1. Create a slash-command context with a `response_url`.
2. Make the `response_url` POST return a non-200 status and a large response body.
3. Call `SlackAdapter.send(...)` for that slash context.
4. The current failure path reads the entire response body before logging `body[:200]` and falling back to success.

## Expected behavior

The failure diagnostic should read only a bounded prefix and release oversized responses.

## Actual behavior

The response_url failure path buffers the whole error body even though the body is only used for a short warning log.

## Impact

This is a narrow reliability hardening issue. Slack response_url failures are non-fatal, but a proxy or Slack edge error returning a large HTML/JSON body can add unnecessary memory and latency during slash-command finalization.

## Proposed fix

Add a Slack-local bounded aiohttp text reader capped at 8 KiB and use it for response_url non-200 diagnostics.

## Validation

I have a focused branch with a regression test proving the failure path avoids `resp.text()`, reads only `limit + 1` bytes, and releases oversized responses.

When a user pastes a long alphanumeric string (e.g., a JWT token) into the Hermes chat, the Agent receives a corrupted version. Characters are dropped and/or substituted, causing the received string to be shorter and garbled. This corruption occurs in the Hermes message delivery layer — **before** the prompt reaches the underlying LLM (llama.cpp).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Generate a long alphanumeric string (JWT token, 2–5 KB). The payload includes a base64-encoded body with a large `dummy_data` field to inflate length.

The string is corrupted **before** it reaches the model:

- **Length reduction:** Characters are dropped (6–8 characters observed in tested cases).
- **Character substitution:** Corruption begins at a consistent position within the payload (~pos 590 in tested JWTs).
- **Cascading corruption:** Because the corrupted portion falls inside base64-encoded content, a shift of even a few characters corrupts the alignment of the entire remaining base64 block.
- **Confirmed pre-model:** An identical JWT pasted directly into the llama.cpp webui repeats perfectly — proving the corruption happens in Hermes, not the LLM.

Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.), Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory), CLI (interactive chat)

The Hermes message delivery pipeline likely performs some form of string truncation, token compression, or reconstruction when handling long alphanumeric content. The corruption pattern (character drops + substitutions within base64-encoded content) suggests one or more of the following:

items.title: [Linux/X11] computer_use tool missing window_id and pid parameters — cannot target specific windows on X11
items.body:
## Environment
- **OS**: Zorin OS 17.3 (Ubuntu 22.04 base, GLIBC 2.35)
- **Session**: X11 (GNOME on Xorg)
- **Hermes**: Desktop, latest
- **cua-driver**: 0.6.8
- **Backend**: X11 via XSendEvent

## Problem
The `computer_use` tool schema does not expose `window_id` and `pid` parameters, which are **required** for targeting specific windows on Linux X11.

### Current schema (from skill docs):
```json
{
  "action": "click",
  "element": 7,
  "coordinate": [100, 200],
  "app": "gedit"
}
```

### Required parameters (cua-driver native):
```json
{
  "pid": 23502,
  "window_id": 58720504,
  "x": 600,
  "y": 500
}
```

## Impact on Linux X11
1. **`app=` parameter ignored** — `computer_use(action="capture", app="gedit")` fails to find window (returns 0x0)
2. **`element=` not functional** — SOM returns 0 elements on X11 (AT-SPI tree doesn't expose X11 window elements)
3. **No way to click/type in specific window** — Must use `cua-driver` CLI directly with `pid` + `window_id`

## Verification
Raw `cua-driver` works perfectly on X11:
```bash
# Find window
xdotool search --onlyvisible --name "gedit"  # → 58720504
xdotool getwindowpid 58720504                 # → 23502

# Click works
cua-driver call click '{"pid": 23502, "window_id": 58720504, "x": 600, "y": 500}'
# ✅ Clicked at (600.0, 500.0) × 1.

# Type works  
cua-driver call type_text '{"pid": 23502, "window_id": 58720504, "text": "hello"}'
# ✅ {"characters": 5, "path": "ax"}
```

## Request
Add `window_id` (integer) and `pid` (integer) parameters to the `computer_use` tool schema for actions: `click`, `double_click`, `right_click`, `drag`, `scroll`, `type`, `key`, `capture`.

This matches the native `cua-driver` MCP tools (`mcp_cua_driver_click`, `mcp_cua_driver_type_text`, etc.) which require both fields on Linux X11.

## Related
- Issue #24170 documents macOS wrapper bugs — this is the **Linux X11 equivalent gap**
- Skill: `skills/computer-use/SKILL.md` documents `app=` but it doesn't work on X11
- Workaround: Use `terminal` tool to call `cua-driver` directly (not ideal)

## Suggested Schema Addition
```json
{
  "click": {
    "parameters": {
      "element": {"type": "integer"},
      "coordinate": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "integer"}},
      "window_id": {"type": "integer", "description": "X11 window ID (from xdotool/list_windows)"},
      "pid": {"type": "integer", "description": "Process ID owning the window"}
    }
  }
  // ... same for other actions
}
```

items.title: Inbound email: a malformed RFC 2047 header crashes _decode_header_value and aborts the IMAP fetch, dropping the message

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
### What happens

`_decode_header_value` in `plugins/platforms/email/adapter.py` decodes RFC 2047 email headers but does not handle malformed input:

```python
def _decode_header_value(raw: str) -> str:
    parts = decode_header(raw)   # raises on a malformed encoded-word
    ...
```

`email.header.decode_header` raises `HeaderParseError` on a malformed base64 encoded-word (for example a one-character base64 group), and `bytes.decode` raises `LookupError` for an unknown charset label. Email headers are attacker-controlled, so any sender can put one of these in `From:` or `Subject:`.

`_fetch_new_messages` calls `_decode_header_value` on `From:` (line 681) and `Subject:` (line 686) for every fetched message, with no per-message guard. The only `except` is the function-level one around the whole IMAP session, so the exception aborts the entire fetch batch. The crashing message was already added to `_seen_uids` and fetched with `(RFC822)` (which sets `\Seen`), so it is silently dropped — never delivered to the agent — and the remaining messages in that batch are deferred.

### Reproduction

```python
from plugins.platforms.email.adapter import _decode_header_value
_decode_header_value("=?utf-8?B?a?=")
# email.errors.HeaderParseError: Base64 decoding error
```

A real email with `Subject: =?utf-8?B?a?=` (or that shape in the `From` display name) reproduces it end to end.

### Impact

Any sender can craft a header that crashes the inbound IMAP fetch: that message is consumed (marked `\Seen`) but never delivered, and the rest of the batch is pushed to the next poll. Repeated crafted messages keep disrupting delivery. A legitimate message from a buggy mailer that emits a malformed encoded-word is silently lost the same way.

### Fix

Make `_decode_header_value` resilient: fall back to the raw header when `decode_header` raises, and decode unknown-charset parts as UTF-8 with replacement instead of raising.

items.title: Inbound email: an unknown Content-Type charset crashes _extract_text_body (LookupError) and aborts the IMAP fetch

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
### What happens

`_extract_text_body` in `plugins/platforms/email/adapter.py` decodes the message body using the charset from the `Content-Type` header:

```python
charset = part.get_content_charset() or "utf-8"
return payload.decode(charset, errors="replace")
```

The charset is attacker-controlled. An unknown label such as `charset=bogus` makes `bytes.decode` raise `LookupError: unknown encoding: bogus` — and that happens *before* the `errors="replace"` handler can run, so `errors="replace"` does not protect against it. All three decode sites (plain part, HTML part, and the non-multipart branch) have this.

`_fetch_new_messages` calls `_extract_text_body` for every fetched message (line 705) under only the function-level `try`, so the `LookupError` aborts the whole IMAP fetch batch. The message was already added to `_seen_uids` and fetched with `(RFC822)` (which sets `\Seen`), so it is consumed but never delivered, and the rest of the batch is deferred.

This is the same impact as #55381 but a distinct code path: that one is the header decoder (`_decode_header_value`); this is the body decoder (`_extract_text_body`), triggered by the `Content-Type` charset rather than an RFC 2047 encoded-word.

### Reproduction

```python
import email
from plugins.platforms.email.adapter import _extract_text_body

msg = email.message_from_bytes(b"Content-Type: text/plain; charset=bogus\n\nHello")
_extract_text_body(msg)
# LookupError: unknown encoding: bogus
```

### Impact

Any sender can set `charset` to an unknown label and crash the inbound fetch. The crafted message is dropped (already marked `\Seen`) and never delivered, while the remaining messages in the batch are deferred. A legitimate message from a mailer that emits a non-standard charset label is lost the same way.

### Fix

Decode with a fallback: try the declared charset, and on `LookupError` decode as UTF-8 with replacement.

items.title: [Feature]: Dynamic task complexity router for kanban pipelines

labels.name: sweeper:not-planned
labels.description: Sweeper: closed per standing maintainer policy (design direction)

items.body:
## Problem

The kanban loop engineering pipeline (#53481: analyst -> coder -> reviewer -> QA -> observe) applies the same static decomposition to every task. Simple tasks waste tokens going through the full pipeline; complex tasks may need deeper decomposition than the static config provides. There's no pre-flight complexity assessment.

## Proposed Solution

Insert a lightweight **Router** before the kanban pipeline:

```
Task enters
  -> Router assesses (single lightweight LLM call: title + description + file scope)
  -> Output: { complexity: 1-5, estimated_tokens, mode: "direct" | "decompose" }
  -> direct (complexity 1-2): bypass kanban, execute in main loop
  -> decompose (complexity 3-5): split into sub-tasks, fan out to kanban lanes
```

**Complexity scale:**
| Level | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| 1 | Single file, local change, no dependencies |
| 2 | Multi-file, single module, predictable scope |
| 3 | Cross-module, requires context reading |
| 4 | Cross-repo / cross-language, unknown dependencies |
| 5 | Architectural, requires design decisions |

## Why

- **Token savings**: simple tasks skip decomposer overhead (estimated 40-60% fewer tokens for complexity-1 tasks)
- **Context hygiene**: single-agent loop for simple tasks, multi-agent only when decomposition adds value
- **Feedback loop**: Router assessments can back-propagate to tune kanban pipeline depth per task class
- The Router itself can use a small model to minimize assessment cost

## Relationship to existing work

- Builds on **#53481** (kanban pipeline) — adds the "should we pipeline?" decision layer
- Complements **#26675** (Managed Agent Runtime) — a concrete routing primitive
- Does not change the kanban pipeline itself — purely an upstream routing decision

items.title: desktop: bundle-electron-main.mjs overwrites tracked electron/main.cjs in place, dirtying the tree and blocking git auto-update

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

items.body:
## Summary

`apps/desktop/scripts/bundle-electron-main.mjs` bundles `electron/main.cjs` **in place**, overwriting a git-tracked file with esbuild output (`renameSync(tmp, entry)` at line 31). When the freshly-bundled bytes differ from what's committed, the desktop build leaves the working tree dirty. On installs that auto-update via `git`, the updater's dirty-tree guard then **refuses to pull** and the agent silently stops receiving updates.

This is a build-system hygiene issue (build output written over tracked source), independent of *which* content is committed — so it is **not** resolved by #54676 (which re-baselines the committed bundle but keeps the in-place overwrite).

## Repro

```bash
cd apps/desktop
git status --porcelain apps/desktop/electron/main.cjs   # clean
npm run build                                            # runs bundle-electron-main.mjs
git status --porcelain apps/desktop/electron/main.cjs   #  M electron/main.cjs  ← tree now dirty
```

Any git-based auto-updater that gates on a clean tree (e.g. a `git fetch && reset/pull`-style updater that refuses to clobber uncommitted changes) then blocks on the next cycle until someone runs `git checkout -- apps/desktop/electron/main.cjs`.

## Root cause

`apps/desktop/scripts/bundle-electron-main.mjs`:

```js
const entry = resolve(root, 'electron/main.cjs')        // line 16 — TRACKED source/entry
const tmp   = resolve(root, 'electron/main.bundled.cjs') // line 17
await build({ entryPoints: [entry], outfile: tmp, /* … */ })
renameSync(tmp, entry)                                   // line 31 — clobbers the tracked file
```

`package.json` has `"main": "electron/main.cjs"`, so Electron loads that exact path — which is why the bundler targets it in place today.

## Interaction with #54676

#54676 ("refresh bundled electron main entrypoint") commits the *bundled* form of `main.cjs` and relaxes the desktop tests to tolerate bundled output. That removes the dirty-tree symptom **only while** the committed bytes happen to match a local rebuild. The moment esbuild output drifts (esbuild version bump, `target`/platform differences, Node minor), `renameSync` re-dirties the tree and the auto-update block returns. The two changes are complementary, not substitutes: #54676 chooses *what* is committed; this issue is about *not writing build output over a tracked path at all*.

## Proposed fixes (either resolves it durably)

**Option A — build to an ignored path, package from there.** Emit the bundle to e.g. `apps/desktop/build/electron/main.cjs` (gitignored), point `electron-builder`'s packaged entry at the built file, and keep `electron/main.cjs` as the un-bundled dev/test entry for `electron .`. Cleanest separation of source vs artifact; the tracked tree never goes dirty from a build.

**Option B — keep committing the bundle (the #54676 direction) but add a write-guard.** Before `renameSync`, refuse to overwrite a path that is git-tracked *and* would change, unless an explicit `--write-tracked`/`REBUNDLE=1` flag is set; otherwise write to `tmp` and exit non-zero with a message telling the dev to commit the regenerated bundle deliberately. This catches the "dev ran `npm run build` and silently dirtied the tree" footgun at build time instead of at update time.

Recommendation: **Option A** is the more robust long-term fix (source and artifact in separate trees), but **Option B** is the smaller change and aligns with the direction #54676 has already taken. A maintainer steer on which is preferred would let this be a tight, single-purpose PR.

## Environment

- macOS, desktop app installed with git-based auto-update.
- Observed live: a desktop `npm run build` on 2026-06-26 left `apps/desktop/electron/main.cjs` modified (esbuild bundle, ~12k lines vs the committed source), which blocked the git auto-updater's dirty-tree gate for ~2 days until the file was restored with `git checkout`.

Happy to open a PR for whichever option a maintainer prefers.
